newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea grills president's son as criminal suspect.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea grills president's son as criminal suspect.

text.p: State prosecutors said they began questioning South Korean President Kim Young-sam's son on Thursday on suspicion of taking kickbacks and peddling influence.
"Mr Kim Hyun-chul is being questioned as a suspect," one prosecution official told reporters.
"Prosecutors have secured enough evidence that he violated laws," another prosecution official told Reuters. "We have drawn up questions aimed at securing his confession."
Earlier, television pictures showed Kim Hyun-chul arriving at the Supreme Public Prosecutors' Office in Seoul.
Prosecution sources said Kim Hyun-chul, the president's second son, would be arrested soon, probably by Saturday.

Prosecutors said they had traced more than 100 bank accounts of Kim Hyun-chul's close associates and their relatives to find out if the president's son accepted kickbacks in return for peddling influence.
By summoning the president's son, the prosecution has signalled that its probe into a sleaze scandal uncovered by the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co might be approaching the end.

The scandal has caused a political storm in South Korea, dealing a serious blow to the credibility of a president who came to office on an anti-graft ticket. President Kim has been reduced to a lame duck in his last year in office.
During parliamentary hearings over a loans-for-kickbanks scandal surrounding Hanbo, Kim Hyun-chul denied last month he took bribes from companies or meddled in state affairs.
Kim Hyun-chul, who helped engineer his father's victory in the 1992 presidential election, is also under investigation over allegations he had kept some unspent election campaign funds.

The main opposition National Congress for New Politics party has alleged Kim Hyun-chul pressured banks to provide loans to Hanbo in return for a donation worth tens of billions of won to help finance the 1992 campaign. The younger Kim has denied this.
Financing of the 1992 campaign and the Hanbo scandal have emerged as the most explosive political issues in the run-up to presidential elections in December.
President Kim, whose five-year term expires next February, is barred by the constitution from seeking re-election.
South Korean prosecutors have traditionally announced the summoning of suspected criminals only when they have secured evidence to charge them.
"Kim Hyun-chul is not an exception. He will face legal action if any wrongdoing is found," a prosecution spokesman said.

Senior prosecutor Shim Je-ryoon said on Wednesday that Kim Hyun-chul had received 60 million won ($67,000) a month from each of three companies between mid-1993 and late 1995. Shim did not say what the money was for.

Kim Hyun-chul, the first son of a South Korean incumbent president to be probed for criminal offences, was questioned by prosecutors in February on whether he pressured banks to keep loans rolling to Hanbo. He was not a suspect at that time.

Hanbo Steel, South Korea's second largest steelmaker, folded in January under debts of five trillion won. The failure brought to light a web of corrupt alliances beteen politicians, businessmen and bankers.

Prosecutors have previously exonerated Kim Hyun-chul over the Hanbo scandal for which 11 people are on trial. They include a former cabinet minister, presidential aides, ruling and opposition lawmakers, bankers and Hanbo's founder Chung Tae-soo. ($1 = 893 won)
